paras: The shooting and disappearance of a Black man near Sycamore, Georgia, took place in June 1888, after J. F. Horkan shot an unnamed "negro man" accused of making "insulting proposals" to a white girl in his household. Neighbors threatened to lynch the wounded man, but Horkan refused; days later the man vanished, and it was "generally supposed he was lynched."
While the Horkans were away, a Black man from an adjoining place came for water and, the accounts say, made "insulting proposals" to a girl of about 13 living with them.

When the girl told the Horkans, Horkan went after the man and fired four times, striking him twice. The neighbors "threatened to lynch him and finish the work," but Horkan would not let them touch him and said he would give him "a chance for life."

According to the Worth Local of Sumner, the man went to Jehu Branch's place in Irwin county on a promise to leave the community if he recovered. Calling him guilty of earlier "meanness" and disliked by white and Black residents alike, the paper said Branch ordered him off, and a day or two after returning to Sycamore he "mysteriously disappeared."
His father could not find him after a diligent search and, the Worth Local said, seemed "indifferent" to his fate. No report of a body, an inquest or an arrest appears, and the man was never named.

The Savannah Morning News first ran the story on June 15 as a "sensation" among Georgia briefs, crediting news that reached Albany. The Atlanta Constitution reprinted it in its "Through Dixie" roundup on June 19. On June 24 the Morning News printed the Worth Local's fuller account, which noted the supposed lynching in passing. None of the papers commented on the lynching threat, and all called the man only "the negro."

The first report placed the wounds in the man's side and chest; the Worth Local put them in his back and hip. The first report set the affair in Irwin county; the Worth Local wrote of Sycamore and "the edge of Irwin county" as separate.

accounts.label: First report (news reaching Albany)
accounts.gist: Horkan shot the man after the girl's complaint; neighbors threatened lynching but Horkan spared him to give him 'a chance for life'.

accounts.label: Worth Local (Sumner)
accounts.gist: Adds that the man was sent to Branch's place, ordered off, returned to Sycamore and disappeared, and that it was 'generally supposed he was lynched'.

framing.detail: The Morning News ran the item as a 'sensation' among state news briefs, with no comment on the threatened lynching.
The Atlanta Constitution reprinted the same text in its 'Through Dixie' roundup as 'a report of a sensation in Irwin county'.
The Worth Local version, reprinted by the Morning News, reports the supposed lynching flatly while stressing the man's earlier 'meanness' and that he was disliked by white and Black citizens.

info: Shooting took place before Wednesday, June 13, 1888, when news reached Albany; the Worth Local dated it 'a week or two since'. The disappearance followed 'a day or two' after the man returned to Sycamore, before June 24.
Home of J. F. Horkan, in Irwin county near Sycamore, Georgia; the man later disappeared after returning to Sycamore.
An unnamed 'negro man from an adjoining place'; his father and a brother are mentioned.
Accused of making 'insulting proposals' to a white girl of about 13 who lived with the Horkans, while he came to the house for water.
J. F. Horkan shot him; 'the neighbors' threatened to lynch him. No one is named as responsible for the supposed lynching.
Unknown; 'generally supposed he was lynched', not confirmed.
He disappeared a day or two after returning to Sycamore; his father could not find him after 'diligent search'.
